title: Suggested self-care/leisure activities list
description: This latent fires on phrases that enumerate concrete self-care, relaxation, or creative activities as suggestions—e.g., 'yoga, meditation, journaling,' 'drawing, painting, writing,' 'take a walk, read a book'—typically in advice-giving contexts recommending stress relief, hobbies, or wellness routines. It activates most strongly on list-like or example-laden recommendations naming specific leisure/wellness actions (exercise, mindfulness, art, nature, breaks), especially when phrased as 'this could include X, Y, or Z' or bulleted activity suggestions. It does not activate on general advice about communication, relationships, self-reflection, or abstract encouragement (e.g., 'be yourself,' 'focus on your strengths') that lacks a concrete named activity, nor on narrative or factual statements unrelated to self-care activity lists.

title: Rhetorical framing exclamation for interpersonal dilemmas
description: This latent fires on short, stock exclamatory openers that frame an upcoming discussion of an interpersonal or relational problem as a familiar, recurring type of situation, typically using phrases like 'The age-old dilemma!', 'The classic conundrum!', or 'The eternal debate!' It activates most strongly on formulaic 'The [adjective] [noun]!' constructions (age-old, classic, eternal, delicate, complex) referring to dilemmas, debates, dynamics, or drama—especially around roommates, family, siblings, pets, and relationships—used as a rhetorical throat-clearing device before advice or analysis. It activates more weakly on similar sentences embedded mid-paragraph or that add extra descriptive clauses (e.g., 'The age-old conundrum of dealing with dishonesty in a relationship!'), and does not activate on sentences that give direct advice, empathetic statements ('I understand your concern'), or substantive content without this exclamatory naming-the-dilemma framing.

title: AITA verdict-prompt question
description: This latent fires on the recurring rhetorical question that opens or closes an AITA (Am I The Asshole) style judgment, typically phrased as 'So, are you the asshole?' or the abbreviation 'AITA?'. It activates most strongly on this exact templated interrogative, including minor grammatical variants (was/were/am you the asshole) and close paraphrases like 'are you being unreasonable' or 'are you in the wrong,' especially when prefaced by the discourse marker 'So,' signaling a transition into a final verdict. It activates more weakly on related AITA-genre content such as verdicts, justifications, and advice statements (e.g., 'you're not the asshole', 'NTA', explanations of who is to blame), but these score lower than the direct question form itself. It would not activate on unrelated questions or on AITA discussion that doesn't pose or echo this specific 'am I the asshole' query structure.

title: List-item numbering and short check-in questions
description: This latent fires on short, standalone tokens that serve as discrete list markers (bare numerals like '2.', '3.', '4.') and on brief, formulaic conversational check-in or prompting phrases ('Is everything okay?', 'What do you think?', 'Have you been feeling okay?'). It seems to capture very short, self-contained utterances that function as structural or turn-taking markers rather than substantive content: either enumerating items in a numbered list or soliciting a quick reaction/confirmation from the listener. It does not activate on longer, content-rich advice sentences, explanations, or multi-clause statements even when they discuss similar emotional check-in topics (e.g. 'It's natural to worry about a loved one's health...'), since those carry substantive semantic content rather than being a bare numeral or short formulaic prompt.

title: Empathetic acknowledgment openers
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic phrases expressing immediate empathetic validation, typically opening a response, such as 'I totally understand your concerns!' or 'I completely understand your struggle.' It activates most strongly on the canonical templates 'I (totally/completely) understand/get it [+ your concern(s)/struggle/dilemma/frustration]', especially with an exclamation point signaling enthusiastic reassurance. It generalizes weakly to other empathy-signaling openers ('It's completely reasonable...', 'It's understandable that...', 'What a complicated situation!') but activates far more weakly on these than on the exact 'I understand/get it' formula. It does not activate on substantive advice, analysis, or judgments (e.g., NTA verdicts, suggestions, questions) that lack this specific direct empathetic acknowledgment phrasing.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on standalone numeral tokens (e.g., '2.', '3.', '4.') that mark items in an enumerated list, typically in advice or reasoning responses that break points into numbered steps or bullet points. It activates most strongly on the bare digit-plus-period token itself, regardless of the list's topic or content. It would not activate on the prose content following the numbers (the actual reasoning, advice, or claims), nor on ordinal words spelled out in text (e.g., 'firstly', 'secondly') or list introductions like 'Here's why:' -- it is specifically tied to the numeral marker token, not the surrounding list structure or semantics.

title: Advice-list preamble framing
description: This latent fires on the formulaic introductory phrases that preface a list of suggestions, steps, or compromises in advice-giving text (e.g., 'Here are some suggestions to help you navigate this situation:', 'Here's a possible solution:', 'Consider a compromise'), as well as short standalone directives urging compromise or conversation ('Perhaps a compromise could be reached', 'Work together to find a compromise'). It activates most strongly on the templated lead-in sentence itself (often ending in a colon before an enumerated list), and also more weakly on generic compromise/resolution-oriented statements. It does NOT activate strongly on the substantive advice content that follows the colon, on numbered list items themselves, or on other advice-adjacent sentences that discuss reasoning, empathy, or specific relationship details without using this 'here are suggestions / consider the following' framing structure.

title: Positive relational-benefit statements
description: This latent fires on clauses that assert a positive social/emotional outcome of some behavior, typically following a 'This/That can/will help...' template, where the payoff is framed in terms of trust, connection, rapport, understanding, or a stronger relationship. It activates most strongly on short, generic, formulaic sentences summarizing the interpersonal benefit of an action (e.g. 'This can help build trust and strengthen your bond'), including occasional negative-outcome mirror cases (e.g. damaging trust) that use the same 'this can lead to X relational effect' structure. It does not activate on sentences giving concrete advice, asking clarifying questions, describing specific situations/scenarios, or offering nuanced discursive reasoning about a relationship problem -- i.e., the surrounding advice-column narrative, empathetic validation, or situational detail found in the random sample, which lacks the compact 'X leads to/helps relational-benefit Y' generalization pattern.

title: Advice on using 'I' statements calmly
description: This latent fires on advice-giving text that recommends using 'I' statements to express feelings/emotions while avoiding blaming, accusing, or attacking language, typically in the context of interpersonal or relationship communication tips. It also activates on numbered/bulleted list markers (e.g., '2.', '3.') that introduce such advice steps in structured how-to responses about calm, respectful, honest communication. It is most strongly tied to the specific phrasing pattern 'Use "I" statements to express your X and avoid blaming/accusing/attacking language,' and to list-item numbers preceding this kind of advice. It does NOT activate as strongly on general relationship advice that lacks this 'I statement' framing or explicit avoid-blame construction, such as suggestions to have an open conversation, acknowledge feelings, or practice self-compassion, even though these are topically similar communication tips.

title: Formulaic self-care affirmation closers
description: This latent fires on stock, therapeutic-sounding affirmation formulas that reassure the reader of their worth and grant permission to prioritize their own needs, feelings, or well-being ('you deserve...', 'remember, you are strong and capable...', 'take care of yourself and prioritize your own well-being'). It activates most strongly on short, templated, sentence-final validating statements that follow a near-identical script of self-worth + permission-to-prioritize-self, often used as closing lines in advice/support responses. It is much weaker or absent on sentences that give concrete advice, analyze a situation, describe other people's behavior, or use similar vocabulary (boundaries, well-being, prioritize) but in a discursive/explanatory rather than direct-address affirmational tone (e.g., 'it's essential to prioritize your own emotional well-being' embedded in reasoning, or third-person statements about other people's feelings). Plain lists, feedback suggestions, or situational analysis without the direct reassuring 'you are/you deserve' framing do not trigger it strongly.

title: Numbered list markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral or bullet marker that begins an item in an enumerated or numbered list (e.g., '3.', '4.', '9.'), often followed by bold formatting markers ('**'). It activates most strongly on isolated digit tokens at the start of list items, regardless of the list's topic, and appears agnostic to whether the surrounding content is advice, options, or steps. It would not activate on ordinary prose sentences lacking a leading list-number token, even if they discuss similar advice-giving or enumerative content, and it is distinct from the semantic content of the list items themselves (e.g., boundary-setting advice, relationship guidance).
